_help: Optional prose rendered on the site. Each section takes 'simple' (plain language, default view) and 'advanced' text; Markdown subset: blank line = new paragraph, **bold**, *italic*, `code`, [link](https://…). Empty strings are ignored. luna.best: run label, display name or variant id to highlight as the configuration confirmed on the test split (otherwise the export's 'confirmed' flag is used). luna.takeaway: replaces the auto-generated Luna takeaway in the simple view.

formats.simple:
We tested GPT-6 Luna in four kinds of games: **cash games** (deep stacks), **tournaments** at 40 and 20 big blinds, and **Spin & Go** (very short stacks). After the flop, Luna loses the most in deep cash games, where pots get big and mistakes are expensive, and the least in short-stacked games. Before the flop it is the other way round: it plays deep stacks fine but used to be its worst with short stacks — until we told it one sentence about short-stack strategy (see Part 4).

**When all five models agree, they're usually right.** On the 200-spot test, unanimous picks lost very little (0.55% of the pot per decision); when the models split 3–2 the loss was eight times higher. A simple majority vote of the five beat even the best single model (1.99% vs 2.57%).
formats.advanced:
Postflop numbers come from full-hand suites (flop solves from preflop ranges, every decision of both seats on flop/turn/river, no triviality filter); preflop numbers from heads-up preflop suites (exact push/fold Nash ≤12bb, equity-realisation tree deeper). Tournament formats are chip EV — ICM is not modelled. bb/100 lost = Σ EV loss per hand ÷ 2 seats, 95% CI over hands; it is dominated by a few large-pot mistakes, so EV loss in % pot is the steadier per-decision metric.

Cross-model analysis (200-spot suite, v2, plurality of argmax picks): 5/5 agree on 35% of spots (pick best 80%, mean loss 0.55% pot), 4/5 28% (81%, 1.22%), 3/5 28% (58%, 4.43%), 2/5 9% (61%, 2.54%). Majority vote 1.99% pot vs Luna 2.57%. Pairwise agreement 55% (Luna–Mercury) to 74% (Jev–d1). Share of EV loss from bet-sizing (right action type, wrong size): Luna 34%, Mercury 27%, Jev 20%, d1 11%, Clef 5%.

arena.simple: Here the models played **whole hands** against two computer opponents: a solid 'regular' (TAG bot) and a 'calling station' that never folds. **No model beat the solid regular** — GPT-6 Luna broke even and Mercury came close. Against the calling station every model won, and most won *more* than the solid bot does, because they bet a lot and that is exactly how you beat someone who never folds. Luna was the exception: careful and balanced, it barely exploited the weak player. For scale: the solid regular bot beats a maniac by about 240 and a random player by about 330 big blinds per 100 hands, while the calling station only breaks even against them. Across all games, the decision models rate about the same as the solid regular bot.
arena.advanced: Duplicate format (each deal played twice with seats swapped), 100bb, blinds 0.5/1. Models were run with the default state (pre-optimisation). bb/100 CIs are wide at 300–500 hands; the TAG bot's own +242 bb/100 vs the station is the reference. `~plus` rows = the same model with the benchmark-confirmed nut-ranking facts (short-stack advice never triggers at 100bb). Bot calibration (400 deals, duplicate): TAG vs maniac +238 ± 187, TAG vs random +334 ± 127, station vs maniac −28 ± 227, station vs random +30 ± 300. Bradley–Terry ratings (all saved matches): d1 1594, TAG bot 1589, Luna 1570, Mercury 1568, Clef 1529, Jev 1442, maniac 1393, random 1342, station 1330 (Luna ~plus 1619 from a single 100-deal match).

luna.simple:
We tried many ways of describing the same poker spot to GPT-6 Luna and kept only what improved it on hands it had **never seen** (a separate test set). Two changes stood out:

After the flop, telling Luna **how close its hand is to the best possible hand** (and its chance to win against the hands the opponent is likely to hold) cut its mistakes by about **30%** in cash games and **30–40%** in tournaments and Spin & Go.

Before the flop with short stacks, **one sentence of standard short-stack advice** ("limp, fold or go all-in; small raises are rarely right") roughly **halved** its losses in Spin & Go. Without it, Luna never went all-in preflop.

Things that did *not* help: theory-heavy coaching, asking the same question three ways, yes/no questions per action, and giving less information. Even improved, Luna still loses to perfect play — just much less.

**It's not just Luna.** We gave the same "what beats me" description to three cheaper models. All of them improved, and the cheapest (Mercury Decide, about a fifth of Luna's price) jumped from 79 to 91 points — catching up with Luna. How you describe the situation to these models matters about as much as which model you pick.

**But perfect-play scores don't automatically win money.** When we replayed full hands against the solid regular bot, the improved models did not win measurably more (Luna +13 vs +4, Mercury −34 vs −7 big blinds per 100 hands, both within the margin of error). Playing closer to perfect play and beating a particular opponent are different skills.

**The models know when they're unsure.** When Luna puts more than 80% on one move, it picks the best move 78% of the time; when it's split (40–60%), only 53%, and those decisions cost about three times as much. A real bot could use that signal to double-check its shaky decisions.

**A cheap model can match the best one.** With the improved description, Mercury Decide played as well as GPT-6 Luna on 300 tournament decisions (89 vs 89 points) for one fifth of the price.

**Ask for a second opinion only when unsure.** Letting another model decide Luna's least-confident 1–5% of moves cut its mistakes by about 12%; handing over more than that made things worse.
luna.advanced:
Protocol: variants tuned on the cash dev split (337 decisions), confirmed on the held-out test split (324 decisions) and then on independent MTT 40bb / MTT 20bb / Spin full-hand suites and two independent Spin preflop suites. Postflop winner `nuts` = `eqrange` (Monte-Carlo equity vs the villain's preflop range narrowed by its actions with a strength heuristic — no solver data) + exact nut ranking (number of villain holdings that beat hero now) + one sentence on value extraction with strong hands. Test split: EV loss 2.19% → 1.52% pot (paired Δ −0.67 ± 0.65%, significant), bb/100 lost 179 → 142. MTT40 89 → 55, MTT20 56 → 40, Spin 46 → 28 bb/100 lost (all paired-significant). Preflop winner `shortstack` (≤30bb: v2 + one sentence of short-stack guidance): Spin preflop score 75.7 → 87.2 and 71.0 → 84.6 on an independent suite; MTT20 71.4 → 84.0 (all significant). Equity facts *hurt* preflop (eq/coach significantly worse than v2). Sharpening Luna's distribution (τ = 4) makes its mixed strategy nearly as good as its argmax (cash test 3.36% → 2.36% pot). Ensembles of Luna variants and `multi`/`noul` gave no reliable gain; the fold guardrail never triggered. Recommended configuration: **`nuts` postflop + `shortstack` preflop (v2 preflop when deeper than 30bb)**.

Generalisation (MTT 20bb full hands, first 150 decisions, v2 → nuts): Mercury Decide 4.25% → 1.97% pot (score 78.6 → 90.5), Jev 2.86% → 1.70% (85.0 → 88.7), d1 2.44% → 1.81% (85.6 → 89.1), Luna 2.49% → 1.86% (300 decisions). Postflop breakdown of Luna nuts vs v2 across all four formats (1,231 decisions): facing a bet −50% EV loss (4.01 → 1.99% pot); monsters (>85% equity) remain the largest leak at 5.2% pot (from 7.7%); river 2.3% vs flop/turn ~1.5%. Arena transfer (100bb full hands vs TAG bot, identical deals, `~plus` = nut ranking + value guidance): Mercury −7.4 ± 61.5 → −33.9 ± 57.9 bb/100 (250 deals), Luna +4.0 ± 33.0 → +12.7 ± 43.8 (100 deals) — no significant change: lower EV loss vs GTO does not by itself translate into higher win-rate against an exploitable bot at these sample sizes.

Calibration (all stored Luna answers, n = 8,865): top-probability > 80% → best action 78%, mean loss 3.0% pot; 60–80% → 69%, 4.8%; 40–60% → 53%, 8.7%; < 40% → 32%, 39.9% (n = 28). Jev and d1 show the same monotone pattern (> 80%: 86% / 80% best, 0.7% / 1.3% pot loss); Clef rarely exceeds 60% confidence. Confidence is therefore a usable abstain/escalate signal.

Mercury Decide on all 300 MTT 20bb decisions: v2 → nuts score 80.8 → 88.9, EV loss 3.71% → 2.09% pot, bb/100 lost 82.7 → 43.8 (all paired-significant); Luna nuts 88.7 / 1.86% / 39.7 at 5× the cost. Escalation simulation (150 decisions all four cheap models answered, nuts): Luna alone 1.56% pot; escalate to any model when Luna's top probability < 0.5–0.6 (1–5% of decisions) → 1.37–1.38%; at < 0.7 → 1.35–1.58%; at < 0.8 (30%) → 1.58–1.88%; averaging all four 1.78%. Breakdown of Luna nuts (1,231 postflop decisions): out of position 1.73% vs in position 1.53%; 3-bet pots 1.82% vs single-raised 1.60%; Spin 15bb heads-up 2.46% (no gain from nut facts at 13bb stacks) vs Spin 25bb 1.09% (from 3.06%).
luna.takeaway: Two small, legitimate additions made GPT-6 Luna much better: telling it how close its hand is to the nuts (≈30–40% fewer postflop losses) and one sentence of short-stack advice (≈half the preflop losses in Spin & Go).
